title: Remotes: clone, fetch, pull, push and tags

videos.script: Lesson 1 said every copy of a Git repository is complete. That is true, and it raises a practical question. If everybody has a complete history, how does anybody's work reach anybody else? {{question}} The answer is a copy that the whole team agrees to meet at. On a server, always on. Git calls it a remote, and by habit the first one is called origin. {{origin}} Four verbs move work between your copy and that one. Clone makes your copy in the first place. Push sends your commits up. Fetch brings everybody else's commits down. And pull brings them down and joins them to your work in one go. {{verbs}} The part that surprises people is that nothing happens on its own. Git never checks the server in the background. Until you fetch, your copy believes the server looks exactly as it did last time. {{nothing}} And when two people push to the same branch, the second one is refused, politely, and told what to do. {{refused}} By the end of this lesson, you will know what that message means, and why it is Git protecting your colleague's work. {{title}}
